beats.narration: Ask most tools to make it pop, and they will — brighter, louder, and measurably worse for learning. Ask Medhavy, and something more interesting happens: it does what the theory says, and shows you its reasoning.

Accessibility isn't a review step here — it's a generation default. WCAG two point two double-A contrast, captions, structure, enforced before the artifact exists. Colorblind-safe palettes, calm grounds, one accent.

Sequencing follows the arc — hook, predict, struggle, reveal, apply — because prediction error is what makes memory stick. And cognitive load has rules: one idea per beat, signal don't decorate, no redundancy.
Facts get checked before render, every stated magnitude carries a source, and single-source findings carry a flag that says so. You saw one in video two — flagged on screen, on purpose.

Quick prediction: how many design decisions does one ninety-second reel make? Pick a number and hold it... This one logged more than a dozen. And that's the point — you can count them, because they're written down.

beats.narration: This is what control looks like: one line, addressed to a decision by its ID. No regenerate roulette, no starting over. Change D fourteen — and only D fourteen changes.
Any C L I works — Claude Code, Codex, whatever ships next year. The workflow is deliberately tool-agnostic, because your judgment shouldn't be locked to our interface. The decision log is the API.

beats.narration: Patch, never regenerate. Override a palette and only the affected beats re-render. Every other choice you've made survives. Your course stops being a slot machine.
Now predict the hard case. You override an accessibility default — contrast drops below double-A. What should the system do? Refuse you? Comply silently? Commit to an answer before I show you ours.

It dissents, then complies — and logs it. Contrast now three point eight to one, below double-A, flagged, complied. The log is how pick and override are the same muscle: you change a decision by ID, the receipt is automatic. Defaults without overrides are paternalism. Overrides without memory are amnesia.

Why this matters to the business: creators leave tools that patronize them, and distrust tools that forget. Selection and override are the same muscle — control with a receipt. That's the retention story.

beats.narration: Ask any AI to build you a course, and it will — in minutes. Here's the question that decides whether it's worth anything: what did it start from? This playlist is a pitch, and the pitch fits in one sentence. Watch.
First, the part that's already true: anyone with Claude, or any C L I, can make a real course today. Generation is a commodity now. That's not our product — that's our premise.
But garbage in, garbage out cuts both ways. A blank prompt inherits whatever the prompter happens to know. Most AI courseware starts from thin air — and it shows on the exam, not in the demo.

Medhavy is a connector, not another app — like Higgsfield for cinema. Settings, Connectors, paste one URL: your Claude now has a pantry. Vetted claims, exercises built for struggle, sources attached. The same chef. Better ingredients.

And the design decisions? Made by learning science before you arrive — accessibility, palettes, sequencing, cognitive load — each one applied silently and logged loudly, with its reason, in a file you can read.

beats.narration: The only honest question in a subscription pitch. Generation is a commodity — models will keep making it cheaper. So what, exactly, is the money for? Hold your guess from video one.

The shape is proven: Midjourney and Higgsfield sell subscriptions and credits on top of commodity generation — connect, create, pay for the difference. We take the shape, and change what the difference is.

props.sparkLine: The starting point is the product.

beats.narration: What the money buys is the starting point — the ingredients and the choosing of them, never the finished meal. The vetted spine instead of a blank prompt. Learning-first defaults instead of engagement-shaped ones. The decision log instead of an unexplained artifact. Exercises built in, because the learning loop is part of the product.

And the timing: the substrate went mainstream. Claude for Education has run since April twenty twenty-five — Canvas, Panopto, and Wiley already connect. As of July twenty twenty-six, Claude is free for U.S. K-through-12 teachers. Two lanes of buyers are arriving: program builders who want the market — to pick, inspect, and log — and busy teachers who want delivery, with a receipt. Same pantry, different checkout.
Predict our cost of distribution in tracks one and two. Remember — the product is a URL in a settings page. No procurement, no pilot committee. Adoption is the review.

The institutional lane comes last, on purpose — entered with usage evidence, not ahead of it. Assume every university's opening posture is: not approved for our data. Then arrive with track-two numbers instead of promises.

beats.narration: No download, no dashboard, no new habits to learn. Settings, Connectors, paste one URL — and your Claude just grew a curriculum spine. That's the entire onboarding. Let me show you why that's the moat.
Higgsfield proved the shape for cinematic media: a remote MCP any Claude user adds in three steps. No procurement meeting, no sales call, no pilot committee. The connector is the distribution.

The pantry layer: four tools, returning data, not prose. List what exists. Get the spine for a topic and level. Get the video for a concept. Get exercises by chapter and mix. Versioned, patchable — the chef's mise en place, served over MCP.

One hard rule, covering both layers: no corpus, no serving. Ask for a topic that isn't there, and Medhavy says so — it won't invent, and it won't serve stale. We don't call frozen catch of the day. In education, refusing to improvise is a feature you can sell.

The lane already exists. Anthropic ships education connectors today — Canvas by Instructure, Panopto, Wiley. Claude is the front end; vendors serve content through MCP. Medhavy speaks the substrate's native protocol.

Three tracks, rising friction. A local server on your own machine — days. A public connector anyone can add — weeks. Institutional, through procurement — quarters. Predict which two earn the right to attempt the third... exactly.

props.command: why does AI courseware demo so well and teach so little?
props.runningText: checking the exam, not the demo…
output: the starting point is the gap

beats.narration: Here's a puzzle worth an investment thesis: AI tutoring demos beautifully, learners genuinely love it — and then the exam disagrees. Why?
Education software learned to optimize the wrong thing. Clicks, streaks, completion — learners adore products that don't teach. The market rewarded the demo for twenty years.

patternData.slideMeta: // B02 — THE EVIDENCE · Bastani et al. 2024

beats.narration: One number, carefully sourced. In a randomized study of about a thousand students, GPT-4 practice help lifted practice performance forty-eight percent — and left exam scores seventeen percent worse than the no-AI group. One study — we flag it as one study. But that is the shape of the trap.

Underneath the trap is plumbing: garbage in, garbage out. A blank prompt starts from nothing — no vetted facts, no sequencing, no sources. The model improvises, confidently. Cold generation is the input problem wearing an output costume.
So pause and predict: if the exam keeps disagreeing, what would you fix first — the model, the prompt, or what the prompt starts from? Commit to one.
